turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Tuesday, November 3rd, Election Day in America. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. And we start in Tehran, where Qatari mediators landed on Monday carrying a draft that could either reopen the Strait of Hormuz or run out the clock.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Here's the shape of it. Iran's delegation left the Qatar talks on Sunday after a tense weekend, and by Monday the Qatari mediators were back in Tehran. Iran's foreign minister described a plan that runs over 2 days: on day 1 the United States implements a set of measures, and in return Iran reopens the Strait of Hormuz. The catch is in his own wording, that it depends on American compliance.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the strait is not a theoretical bargaining chip anymore. The UN says Hormuz shipping has plunged by more than 90%. Iran's president said the supreme leader has granted his government certain authorities in the talks, which suggests Tehran's negotiators have some room to move. This is month 8 of the conflict, and that is a long time to be one signature away from something.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The spoiler is Jerusalem. Reports say Benjamin Netanyahu urged Donald Trump to resume strikes immediately after the midterms, while Trump wants negotiations to play out. And there are reports that Washington has told Gulf allies to prepare for a possible new round of fighting as early as Wednesday, November 4. The Washington Post also reported fresh defensive strikes inside Iran on the eve of the vote.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So the diplomatic window and the political calendar are the same window. Trump said in early October that the US would not attack before the midterms, and he has hinted that escalation afterward stays on the table. Tomorrow morning is the first moment that promise expires.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story, and it's a running one. In Israel, the post-election arithmetic is moving toward Gadi Eisenkot. Avigdor Liberman and Yair Golan said on Monday they will recommend him to form the next government, joining Naftali Bennett. The Joint List and Ra'am met in Nazareth and are leaning toward recommending him too, with 19 Arab-party seats that would take his total to roughly 67, according to one count.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: But the obstacle is in the same sentence. Liberman has said he will not serve in a government that depends on Arab-party support. Shas will recommend Netanyahu, and the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism is undeclared. President Herzog opens consultations on Wednesday, and the Knesset is sworn in on November 10th regardless. The Arab parties also agreed to move to replace Speaker Amir Ohana, which would be an early test of that bloc working together.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, Europe's young people are in the streets. Gen Z protests over the cost of living, school funding and housing have now hit France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Belgium, Spain and Greece. On Halloween, the group Gen Z regelt held rallies in more than 30 German cities, with organizers claiming 120,000 people, and the demonstrations turned violent in places, with officials blaming infiltrators.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: France is the heavier case. The unrest began when the government opened 2027 budget talks, it has produced some of the worst rioting in decades, and this past weekend was the 3rd straight of nationwide rallies. Trade unions in France have called a general strike for November 5th, Spain's follow on the 11th, and student unions in Britain and Italy plan a day of action on November 20th. The Economist's read is that this is cost of living and strained public services, not immigration or religion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Apple and Palantir both reported after the close on Monday, and they tell opposite stories. Apple's fiscal 4th quarter revenue was $114.5 billion, up 12% and above its own guide of 9 to 11%. iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion, up 17%, a September-quarter record, despite supply constraints. Earnings per share were $2.10, up 14%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the detail worth a second look is in the margin. Gross margin was 47.9%, and Apple said about 1 percentage point of that, plus 5 cents of EPS, came from tariff refunds. Strip that out and it is still a beat, but you can see the refunds flowing through the income statement. Apple's fiscal 2026 revenue was a record $479 billion, and this is the first full set of numbers with John Ternus as CEO.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Palantir beat on everything and the stock fell anyway. Revenue was $2.31 billion, up 96% year over year, earnings per share were 44 cents against about 41 expected, and it raised full-year revenue guidance to roughly $8.53 billion with adjusted free cash flow of $4.8 to $5.0 billion. For the first time, US commercial revenue exceeded US government revenue.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The shares dropped about 3% in the regular session to $178.44 and slid roughly another 3.8% after hours. The bear point is that new US commercial contract value grew just 11%, which is the number that says whether a 96% growth rate can last. In a month where the Nasdaq-100 flirted with correction territory, a beat is simply the entry fee.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Australia just raised rates again on Melbourne Cup day. The Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years, and the 5th hike of 2026. The vote was 6 to 3, with 3 board members preferring to hold.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The statement cited elevated inflation, the war in the Middle East and oil prices. The split vote is the story, because it raises the odds of a December pause, and it is the mirror image of the Philippines, where we will get to a central bank that is also hiking and also watching its currency. Macquarie has already said it will pass the 25 basis points through to variable-rate mortgages from November 19th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: To Brazil, where the aftershock of the runoff has taken a diplomatic turn. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost to Lula, left the country for Miami in a chartered plane via northern Argentina and Ecuador, even though a Supreme Court order in a money-laundering probe required him to surrender his passports and stay put. He denies wrongdoing and calls it persecution.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Brazil's foreign ministry received Argentina's chargé d'affaires, María Emilia Cortés, on October 29th, according to government sources, to ask what role Javier Milei's government played. Buenos Aires says there was no request for an explanation. Brazil had already permanently recalled its ambassador in August after Milei insulted Lula, so this lands on a relationship that is already broken.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The tape on Monday was really one number, and it was oil. Crude fell more than 6% on hopes of a US-Iran deal, Brent hit a 2-week low, and the S&P energy sector lost more than 2%. That is the only move big enough to say out loud. Everything else, including the index closes, is on the Markets tab.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: What I find interesting is how unevenly that relief was shared. The Dow finished higher, helped by the oil drop and by companies that burn fuel rather than sell it, while the S&P and the Nasdaq slipped as tech kept bleeding after a bruising October. So the peace trade is real, but it is not rotating money into the AI complex, it is rotating money away from energy.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the 10-year Treasury stayed around 4.90%, still hugging the 5% line even with crude collapsing. If a 6% oil drop cannot pull the long end meaningfully lower, then the bond market is pricing something sticky, term premium, supply, a Fed that held last week with dissents in favor of a hike.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: My opinion is that the market is treating this as a binary on Hormuz that it cannot actually handicap. A fall in oil on a draft proposal that depends on American compliance, with Netanyahu reportedly lobbying for strikes right after the vote, is a price built on a rumor. If the talks stall, that 6% comes back in a morning, and the people who bought the relief are the ones who get hurt.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The watch list is simple. The midterm results overnight, where Democrats are widely expected to win the House and the Senate is in doubt, and then whether Wednesday brings strikes. Markets tend to like gridlock, but it is hard to see anyone having priced a Senate flip alongside a renewed Iran war.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Our deep dive today is a story the Economist handpicked in its Saturday newsletter, headlined, in its words, that the Kremlin is shutting down Russia's last free newspaper. Novaya Gazeta announced on October 30th that it is closing, and its staff say they will switch off the lights in their office on November 9th. Novaya Gazeta Europe, its sister outlet in Latvia, ran the headline, quote, they killed us.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: For listeners who don't carry the history, Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 and became the paper that did what almost nobody else in Russia would, investigative reporting on corruption, the Chechen wars and the security services. Its editor, Dmitry Muratov, shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize. Anna Politkovskaya, its best-known correspondent, was murdered in 2006, and the paper has lost other reporters over the years. It suspended its Russian operations once already, in March 2022.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So what actually happened in October? Based on the Economist's account and the reporting from Meduza and CNN, the pressure came in layers. Management was told on October 19th it would be evicted from its building on Potapovsky Lane. Unidentified people entered the office overnight on October 25th and 26th. The paper had been declared a foreign agent, Novaya Gazeta Europe was already designated undesirable, and Muratov said the paper itself could be designated extremist.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that last point is the one that changes the calculus. A foreign agent label is a tax and paperwork burden. An extremist or undesirable designation turns reading, sharing and donating into possible criminal acts for ordinary Russians. Editor Sergei Sokolov was reportedly also questioned in October about the jailed journalist Oleg Roldugin. Staff framed the closing as their own collective decision, a way to protect people, rather than a legal order.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Here's where I'd push on the framing. It's tempting to read this as a pure censorship story, and it is, but the timing matters. This is happening in the middle of the Ukraine negotiations, with the Kremlin certain that the diplomatic track will not hold it accountable for domestic repression. When the West is bargaining over ceasefire lines, the price of closing the last independent newsroom is close to zero.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter-argument is that the closure is actually a tell about fear. A government that is confident in its war narrative does not need to evict a newspaper. Whatever you think of its reach, Novaya Gazeta was a place where the hard specifics got published, procurement fraud, abuses, names. Take that away and the state loses a source of bad news it didn't control but did at least know about.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's also the model question. Meduza framed its interview with Sokolov around whether the paper can rise from the ashes a third time. The Russian exile press, Meduza, Novaya Gazeta Europe, Dozhd, operates from Riga and Berlin on donations and foreign-hosted sites, and the interesting variable is whether Russians can still reach them. VPN use is the real ceiling.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what does it mean for a listener who works in markets and energy? Two things. One, the information environment on Russian sanctions evasion, energy exports and procurement gets thinner, which means more of what we know comes from satellites, customs data and leaks rather than reporters on the ground. Two, it's a reminder that when a state decides to end a newsroom, it can do it with an eviction notice and a rumor of a designation, no trial required.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The energy story today is in your inbox, a SemiAnalysis note from Sunday titled, the datacenter backlash goes bipartisan. The headline claim is that the 2027 buildout is effectively locked in and the midterms cannot stop it. Roughly 3 quarters of the 33.8 GW due across their top 20 states is already under construction, which keeps them comfortable with a global year of more than 50 GW.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The fight is 2028. Their model has 62.2 GW of US net additions that year, most of it not yet started, and 43.5 GW of that, 70% of the national total, sits in 13 states they track. 10 of those 13 elect a governor today. So Tuesday is not a vote on whether the campuses get built, it is a vote on the terms of the ones that haven't broken ground.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The biggest single risk they name is the Texas freeze. The state has stacked 2 holds, the interconnection-queue audit that began on August 3rd, and a pause on TCEQ permits from September 21st that now reaches onsite power. Texas alone is close to 30% of US gigawatts in 2028. ERCOT is targeting December 10th to file its audit report, but the filing does not by itself reopen permitting, and each permit still needs approval.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is where the governor's race matters. Greg Abbott could reopen once ERCOT and the Water Development Board finish. His challenger, Gina Hinojosa, would impose a moratorium until legislation gives communities a voice, protects household bills and ends the tax incentives. The Texas legislature sits from January 12th to May 31st, 2027, so a freeze held through that session runs about 8 months from September, and closer to a year if you wait for new rules to take effect. That is 5 to 9 months worse than a December restart.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Zoom out to the candidate scoreboard. Of the 20 nominees they track, 9 want a pause on new construction and the other 11 want conditions, split about evenly by party. 15 candidates want datacenters to pay their own grid costs, 12 want the tax breaks ended, and 11 want water use limited or reported. The dollar figures: if every pro-pause candidate won, roughly 30 GW of 2028 capacity sits in those states. If only the conditions-only candidates win, the exposure drops to 5.7 GW, because Ohio and Oregon have pause advocates on both sides.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The distinction I like is pause versus conditions. A pause blocks any project that still needs an approval the state has stopped issuing, and you cannot just move to another state, because everywhere else also needs power, permits and a delivery schedule. Conditions change price and terms, so a developer can fund the upgrade, change the cooling design or sign the community agreement and still proceed. Oregon is the live example, where Governor Kotek expanded the freeze on state land to air and water-discharge permits on October 9th, running through July 1st, 2027.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the lever map is worth memorizing. Governors move fastest, by halting permits an agency has not yet issued and by setting review priorities. Legislatures hold the sales-tax exemption on servers, GPUs, networking, cooling and transformers, which they describe as worth potentially billions of dollars per gigawatt, and only legislatures can write moratoria that outlast an executive order. Utility commissions set deposits, minimum bills, upgrade costs and exit fees, and those commissioners are elected in Georgia, Arizona and Oklahoma.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: They tier the states for you. Tier 1, more than 2 GW unstarted and restrictions likely whoever wins: Texas, Ohio, Arizona, with Georgia a toss-up governor's race plus a Public Service Commission majority on the ballot. Tier 2, 1.5 to 2 GW, where change depends on political control: Pennsylvania's Senate race, or a Democratic win in the Oklahoma governor's race. Tier 3, under 1.5 GW, where tighter rules arrive either way: Illinois, Oregon and Iowa. Indiana, Missouri, Wyoming and West Virginia are left out because Republican control and supportive governors are stable.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magandang umaga ulit sa lahat. Dalawang salita ang pag-aaralan natin ngayon, at parehong galing sa mga balita tungkol sa badyet ng gobyerno. Ang una ay "pagsala."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "pagsala" ay galing sa salitang-ugat na "sala," ang salaan na ginagamit sa pagsasala ng harina, ng tubig, o ng kape. Kapag sinabi nating "pagsala ng badyet," ibig sabihin ay pinipili ang mga item na dapat manatili at inaalis ang mga hindi dapat makalusot.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Mahalaga ang pagkakaiba nito sa "pagbusisi," na napag-aralan na natin. Ang pagbusisi ay masusing pagtingin sa bawat linya, samantalang ang pagsala ay may kasamang hatol, may natitira at may natatanggal. Kaya mas matalas ang dating nito sa mga ulat ng Senado.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pormal ito at madalas mong mababasa sa mga pahayagan. Halimbawa, "Sinimulan ng Senado ang pagsala sa mga bagong proyekto ng DPWH." Sa araw-araw na usapan, mas karaniwan ang pandiwang "salain," gaya ng "Salain mo muna ang tubig bago mo inumin."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay "pagtutuos." Ang ugat nito ay "tuos," na ang ibig sabihin ay ang pagkuwenta at pagbabalanse ng mga account, kaya ang pagtutuos ay ang paghahati-hati ng kuwenta kapag oras na ng singilan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: May dalawang mukha ang salitang ito. Sa negosyo, ang pagtutuos ay ang pormal na pagsusuri ng mga libro at ng mga gastos. Pero sa pulitika at sa pelikula, ito ay ang huling pagtutuos, ang oras ng paniningil, ang labanang nagpapasya kung sino ang mananagot.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya kapag sinabi ng isang senador na "maghaharap tayo sa pagtutuos ng badyet," may bigat iyon na higit pa sa simpleng pagbibilang. Ramdam mo na may mananagot at may mawawalan ng pondo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tandaan natin ang pagkakaiba. Ang "pagsala" ay ang pagpili at pag-alis. Ang "pagtutuos" ay ang paniningil at paghaharap. Pakinggan natin ang dalawa sa balita tungkol sa Pilipinas na susunod.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pormal nang nagsimula ang Senado sa pagsala ng panukalang badyet para sa 2027, na nagkakahalaga ng P7.2 trilyon, mas mataas ng P407 bilyon kaysa sa badyet ngayong taon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ayon kay Senador Ping Lacson, "all means all" ang pagtutuos na ito, kaya pati ang distrito ni Sandro Marcos sa Ilocos Norte, na may pinakamalaking dagdag sa pondong pang-imprastraktura sa bersyon ng Kamara, ay hindi ligtas sa pagsala.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Binigyan naman ni Senador JV Ejercito, ang tagapangulo ng finance committee, ang DPWH hanggang ngayong araw para magsumite ng mga dokumento para sa 6,271 bagong proyekto. Kapag walang sapat na batayan, tatanggalin ang mga ito sa badyet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English for the rest of the beat: the Senate resumes plenary on November 9th, interpellations on the budget begin November 23rd, and Lacson says he wants to restore funding for foreign-assisted projects, loan proceeds plus the government's counterpart, that the purge would otherwise wipe out. The Senate majority bloc is formally behind Ejercito's push, which matters after the fights over insertions and lump sums we've followed all fall.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is the parallel track. On November 3rd her defense asked the Senate court to reject the House prosecution's formal offer of her financial and corporate records, arguing the evidence does not establish unexplained wealth and challenging its relevance and authentication. The House panel has dropped 3 of the 4 articles, and says it will hand tax documents on her and her husband's linked companies to the Bureau of Internal Revenue for possible tax cases.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The court is suspended for budget season and reconvenes on November 9th, with a verdict targeted by December 16th. Conviction requires 16 of the 24 senators, and it would bar her from office for life, which matters because she has said she will run for president in 2028.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And on Thursday, November 5th, the Philippine Statistics Authority publishes October inflation. The BSP's own forecast band is 7.1% to 8.1%, after 7.2% in September and a 50 basis point hike to 5.50%, the 4th in a row. Anything near the top of that range makes it very hard to argue the cycle is over, and the peso, which touched a record P64.17 last week, will trade on that print.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Time for Mandarin, and today's 2 words come straight out of the China story. The first is 只好, zhǐhǎo, an adverb meaning have no choice but to, or can only.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It marks a forced second-best. You wanted option A, it is not available, so 只好 introduces what you do instead. 出口商只好降价来保住订单。(Exporters have no choice but to cut prices to hold on to orders.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Register-wise it is neutral to slightly spoken, and it often travels with 于是 or 所以 earlier in the sentence. Compare it to 不得不, which we've done before, which is heavier and describes an obligation or compulsion. 只好 is more resigned, almost a shrug: well, there's nothing else to do.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it contrasts with 只能, which is flatter and purely about limitation. 只好 carries an emotional color, the sense of reluctance. 市场不好,他们只好推迟计划。(The market is poor, so they had no choice but to delay their plans.) Note that it always takes a verb and almost never appears with a negative.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second word is 承受, chéngshòu, to bear or to withstand. It is formal, written-leaning, and the collocations are the whole point, you承受压力, 承受损失, 承受风险, 承受后果, which is pressure, losses, risk and consequences.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Compare it with 忍受, which is to endure something unpleasant, personal and emotional, like noise or pain, and with 接受, which is to accept. 承受 is about capacity, whether a structure, a person or a balance sheet can hold the load. 利润越来越少,很多工厂已经难以承受。(Profits keep shrinking and many factories can no longer bear it.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the useful frame is 承受得了 and 承受不了, can bear and cannot bear. 如果人民币继续升值,出口企业恐怕承受不了。(If the renminbi keeps appreciating, exporters probably cannot bear it.) That is a very finance-desk sentence and it sets up the story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So just to lock it in, 只好 for the forced second-best, 承受 for what a balance sheet can hold. Both are in the China item that follows.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管私营机构的制造业采购经理指数仍然高于50,出口商为了保住订单,只好降价,利润空间已经难以承受。(Although the private manufacturing PMI is still above 50, exporters have no choice but to cut prices to hold on to orders, and the squeeze on margins is hard to bear.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The numbers behind that sentence. The RatingDog manufacturing PMI, the private survey formerly known as the Caixin PMI, came in at 52.0 for October, a hair below September's 52.1 but above the 51.6 forecast, and the 11th straight month of expansion. Output grew, but export orders rose at a 3-month low pace, and output prices fell after rising in September, because firms are cutting prices to protect sales.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That is the dual-speed story in one release. Volumes are fine, pricing power is not. The official PMI, which we flagged last week, was 49.3, with new export orders at 48.7, the lowest since May. Bloomberg's headline is that the economy had a weak start to the fourth quarter because of exporters, which is the growth pillar everything else now leans on.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the debt-deflation lens makes it worse, because falling output prices against fixed nominal debts is how real burdens rise. A factory that borrowed at last year's margins is repaying with this year's thinner ones.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two policy tells from the weekend. First, the offshore yuan broke through 6.65 per dollar on Friday and regulators responded with a weaker fixing, which SCMP reads as a signal of caution about the speed of appreciation. A strong currency on top of falling prices is the exact combination 承受不了 was built for. 如果人民币升值太快,出口企业恐怕承受不了。(If the renminbi appreciates too fast, exporters probably cannot bear it.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second, SCMP reports that China's central bank and regulators are meeting on stock support after what it describes as a record 12-week slide. Support for equities and a managed brake on the currency at the same time tells me, and this is my read, that Beijing would rather lean on markets than on a bigger domestic stimulus.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start in Venice, because the 61st Biennale is a case study in what happens when an art institution tries to stay above politics. Its international jury resigned en masse in late April, 8 days before the opening, a week after saying it would not consider Russia and Israel for awards. The Biennale responded by scrapping the traditional Golden Lions and replacing them with Visitors' Lions, chosen by public vote.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The show closes on November 22nd, and one account says the awards ceremony has been moved to that date. Treat the date with caution, since only 1 source I found carries it. The structural point holds either way. A jury exists to take responsibility for a judgment. A popular vote is a poll about attendance, and it tends to reward the most photographable pavilion, not the most difficult one. Venice just converted its prize from criticism to crowd control.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now a run of London openings that tell you where curators think the money and the attention are. The National Gallery opens its first-ever Jan van Eyck portrait show on November 21st, running through April 11th, 2027. Tate Britain opens Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant on November 12th, and the Hayward Gallery opens the first UK institutional show of Nan Goldin's photographs since 2002 on November 24th.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: I'd pair Van Eyck and Goldin. One is the founding document of the Western portrait, a painter who made a person look back at you. The other is the photographer who made the unflattering truth about a person into the portrait. Same question 600 years apart, what does a face owe the person looking at it. Those are previews, not reviews, so we will return when the critics have been in. And MoMA PS1 opens Hard Art on November 5th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last item, a centennial. Harry Houdini died in Detroit on Halloween in 1926, and the anniversary has produced séances at his former New York home, 3 of them capped at 13 guests, a Potter and Potter auction of 100 artifacts at the Magic Castle, and a show at the Harry Ransom Center in Austin called Houdini's Library.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Library show is the one I would go to. Houdini was a serious book collector, and the Economist's Saturday newsletter made the sharper point that the great illusionist was also a magician at building a personal brand. His real trick was packaging risk, the straitjacket, the chains, the water torture cell, as a story people would pay to watch. In 2026, that is a business model, not a stunt.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two columns today, and they're on opposite sides of the same question, who is responsible for how things turn out. First, Charles Lane in the Washington Post on Monday, headlined, in effect, that President Trump owns the GOP's midterm meltdown.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Steelmanning Lane. He argues the Republican Party is at risk of utter defeat essentially for one reason, Trump's dysfunctional one-man rule over both the government and his party. And he concedes election results rarely lend themselves to single-cause explanations, but says this year may be the exception. The supporting evidence is the numbers: an NBC poll with Trump's disapproval at a record 60%, a New York Times and Siena poll showing Democrats ahead in several Senate battlegrounds including Michigan, Texas and Maine, and the Economist's own forecast that the auguries are good for Democrats.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So where does it break? Three places. First, it assumes the vote is a referendum, when the map still matters. Post opinion writers have argued that redistricting tilts the House map toward Republicans, and Henry Olsen said in April that a sophisticated new poll gave the GOP some heart. Second, a Supreme Court ruling on coordinated spending may have handed Republicans cheaper ad rates to close the cash gap. Third, even Olsen notes no party sweeps all the seats a baseline analysis says it can win.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: My counter is slightly different. A single-cause story is also a convenient story for the people who want the party to stay the same afterwards. If it is only Trump, then a post-Trump party is a clean reset. But the SemiAnalysis piece we just walked through shows candidates in both parties, 9 of 20 nominees wanting pauses on datacenters, running against the same economy. Some of this is not about any one man. It's about electricity bills.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second column is lighter and it lands differently on the Gen Z protests. Andrew Palmer, the Economist's Bartleby columnist, writes that the quality you should most wish for your children is an internal locus of control, the idea from the psychologist Julian Rotter in the 1960s that you believe your actions shape your outcomes, which is closely linked to agency.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The steelman is strong. Agency is something you can build, and the practical lesson for parents and managers is to hand people real decisions rather than reassurance. It is a better advice column than it looks.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter-take writes itself from this morning's headlines. Tell a 22-year-old in Lyon or Lisbon facing a rent they can't cover that her fate is in her own hands and she will point to the budget the government just opened. Locus of control is partly a belief and partly a fact about the world. When the external factors really are dominating, telling people they have agency can sound like a way of moving the blame.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is probably why Palmer's answer works best at the level of a team or a family, and why it travels worst into a general strike. Both things can be true, and the protesters in Berlin are in some sense proving his point, because marching is what an internal locus of control looks like when it meets a bad market.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: For One Good Thing, a story that started with a doorbell camera. Maren and David Douglass are teachers in Florida, and they noticed on their security camera that a schoolgirl was waiting for the bus every morning at the end of their driveway, sitting in the dirt, with no sidewalk and traffic going by.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So they built her a bench. No announcement, no ask, just a bench at the stop. Then they put a Mini Free Library beside it and stocked it with books, so that waiting for the bus could become time with a book. Other kids on the street began borrowing and returning them, and the videos from their doorbell camera, including the girl's happy dance when she first saw the bench, have been watched by millions.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's nothing else to the story and it doesn't need anything else. Someone noticed a small discomfort and fixed it without being asked.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the show. Go and vote if you're in the States, and if you are not, be kind to someone waiting at a stop this morning. I'm Alex.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And I'm Sam. Thank you for listening to The Morning Commute. We'll see you tomorrow.
